source_user: Define prefill and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Prefill is the initial inference pass over the input prompt. It computes the prompt's hidden representations and typically materializes the per-layer K/V state that later autoregressive decoding reuses. It matters because prompt length and prefill scheduling contribute to time-to-first-token and consume compute and memory. Boundary condition: prompt-token work is parallelizable but not cost-free or universally compute-bound; causal masking, padding, kernel choice, batching, precision, and memory pressure can change utilization, so report measured TTFT and peak HBM for the target runtime.
risks: The prefill bottleneck and its benefit depend on workload shape, implementation, scheduler, and available memory.
evidence_required: Record prompt length, runtime configuration, TTFT breakdown, prompt-token throughput, batch/padding, peak HBM, and K/V allocation across repeated workload cells.

source_user: Contrast prefill with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Prefill consumes the prompt as a sequence in an initial batched pass, computes hidden states and K/V tensors, and then hands the resulting state to one-token-at-a-time decode. A naive no-prefill implementation would repeatedly process the prompt or otherwise feed prompt tokens through the decode path, doing more sequential work and typically increasing time-to-first-token. Boundary condition: this is a conceptual contrast, not a promise of a particular speedup; a valid comparison must hold model, precision, hardware, runtime, scheduler, and request trace fixed, and account for padding, chunked prefill, and memory limits.
risks: A naive baseline may be unsupported or use different kernels and batching, making measured differences non-equivalent.
evidence_required: Use a supported reference where possible and measure TTFT, prompt-token work, throughput, TPOT, peak HBM, batch composition, and failures with identical inputs and configurations.

Boundary condition: the contrast depends on what the reference actually does; do not claim a gain without a matched implementation, and separate effects of padding, batching, chunking, and memory pressure.

evidence_required: Document both execution paths and compare identical prompt traces while measuring TTFT, device time, prompt-token throughput, HBM/KV allocation, queueing, and error events.

source_user: Contrast prefill with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Prefill is a dedicated first pass over all prompt tokens: attention and feed-forward operations produce the initial hidden/K/V state, after which decode appends one generated token at a time. A naive implementation that handles the prompt through the decode loop would expose more sequential steps and repeated overhead, usually worsening TTFT and prompt processing efficiency. Boundary condition: a shorter prompt, low occupancy, or a memory-bound kernel can reduce the practical difference; compare only equivalent model and runtime configurations and measure rather than infer the result.
risks: The apparent speedup can be confounded by different kernels, batching, scheduler policy, or input-transfer costs.
evidence_required: Replay fixed prompts and collect TTFT components, prompt-token throughput, GPU utilization, batch/padding, peak HBM, K/V bytes, and failures for both supported paths.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with prefill. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes or trade-offs are: (1) a long prompt can make prefill dominate TTFT and consume substantial temporary activation and attention memory, reducing room for concurrent decode sequences; (2) aggressive batching or long-context admission can improve aggregate GPU utilization while increasing queueing and tail latency, and may trigger OOM, truncation, or rejection. Mechanism: the runtime runs prompt-token matrix operations and constructs the initial K/V state before decode. Boundary condition: the direction and size of these effects depend on prompt length, batch composition, kernel, precision, and memory budget; measure the actual serving configuration rather than assuming prefill is always compute-bound or beneficial.
risks: Failure behavior depends on scheduler admission, implementation, memory headroom, and whether prompt and decode resources are shared.
evidence_required: Capture per-request TTFT, queueing, prompt length, batch composition, peak HBM, activation/KV allocation, OOMs, truncations, and rejections under controlled prompt-length and concurrency sweeps.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with prefill. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Two trade-offs are: (1) increasing prompt length raises prefill work and usually TTFT, even if the prompt is processed in parallel; (2) packing more prompts into a prefill batch can raise throughput but competes for memory and scheduler time with decode, producing higher TPOT or tail latency. Mechanism: prefill computes prompt representations in bulk and writes K/V entries that decode reads later. Boundary condition: short prompts, low occupancy, padding, or a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel may not realize a throughput gain, so classify the regime from measurements instead of inferring it from the word parallel.
risks: Batching can make aggregate throughput and individual latency move in opposite directions; memory pressure can change the execution regime.
evidence_required: Measure TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, batch tokens, padding, peak HBM, KV occupancy, and failure events across prompt length, arrival rate, and concurrency cells.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with prefill. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes or trade-offs are: (1) a very long prompt can exhaust available HBM when its intermediate state and resulting K/V are allocated, causing admission failure, OOM, or reduced concurrency; (2) prefill work scheduled ahead of decode can improve device utilization but delay active sequences and inflate decode tail latency. Mechanism: causal attention and feed-forward layers transform the prompt into hidden states and K/V blocks for subsequent token generation. Boundary condition: exact memory and latency behavior varies with attention implementation, precision, padding, and chunked-prefill policy; verify those settings before generalizing.
risks: OOM and latency regressions may be scheduler- or kernel-specific and should not be attributed to prefill alone without instrumentation.
evidence_required: Record allocation failures, peak and resident HBM, KV blocks, prefill/decode overlap, per-request TTFT and TPOT, and scheduler delays for repeated controlled workloads.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with prefill. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Two trade-offs are: (1) batching many prompt tokens can raise tokens processed per second but increases memory footprint and may leave less capacity for KV cache and concurrent requests; (2) serializing or prioritizing prefill to protect decode latency can lower utilization and throughput. Mechanism: a prefill pass computes attention and feed-forward outputs for the input sequence and materializes K/V state for decode. Boundary condition: causal masking does not make all prompt work independent, and padding, packing, chunking, or kernel choice can dominate; report measured TTFT and batch-token efficiency for the specific runtime.
risks: Throughput improvements can hide worse p95/p99 latency or lower available concurrency; the scheduler policy is a confounder.
evidence_required: Compare scheduler policies with fixed traces and collect batch token counts, padding, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, tail latency, HBM, KV occupancy, and prefill/decode queue time.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with prefill. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes or trade-offs are: (1) long-context prefill can raise TTFT and peak memory enough to cause OOM, rejection, or eviction of other requests; (2) allowing large prefill batches can maximize device work but starve decode, increasing TPOT and tail latency. Mechanism: the prompt pass computes hidden states and stores per-layer K/V that later decode steps reuse. Boundary condition: chunked prefill or prefill/decode disaggregation changes both contention and memory accounting, so these conclusions apply only to the tested architecture and policy.
risks: Architecture and scheduler changes can reverse observed trade-offs; do not treat one deployment's limits as universal.
evidence_required: Run matched prompt-length and concurrency experiments, recording TTFT, TPOT, p99, throughput, peak HBM, cache events, admission outcomes, and prefill scheduling policy.

source_user: Explain how prefill interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Prefill processes the prompt and is generally parallel across prompt tokens; its cost is dominated by prompt processing and often compute utilization.
corrected_answer: Prefill contributes directly to time-to-first-token because the server must process the prompt before emitting the first token. Processing prompts in batches can improve prompt-token throughput, but it consumes compute and memory and can contend with decode, increasing queueing or TPOT. Mechanism: the pass builds hidden states and initial K/V blocks that subsequent decode reads. Boundary condition: with chunked or disaggregated prefill, contention and latency differ from an integrated scheduler; report prompt length, batch composition, HBM, TTFT, TPOT, and queue time for the chosen design.
risks: Latency, throughput, and memory are coupled through scheduling and batching, so a single aggregate metric can conceal regressions.
evidence_required: Use a fixed trace and sweep prompt length and concurrency while measuring per-request TTFT/TPOT percentiles, throughput, queueing, batch tokens, peak HBM, and KV allocation.
